Purge
PURJ
v.
From Latin purgare, “to cleanse, purify,” from purus (pure) + agere (to drive). Renders the Greek katharizō, “to cleanse,” and the Hebrew kāphar, “to cover, atone,” and tāhēr, “to be clean.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To purge is to cleanse by the removal of what defiles—to drive out the impurity that pollutes, leaving the thing or person pure. In Scripture the verb covers both ceremonial and moral cleansing, and its highest reference is to the purging of sin from the conscience by the blood of Christ. David prays, Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean—the Old Testament rite of cleansing pleaded as a figure of the deeper cleansing he longs for. The writer to the Hebrews sets the doctrine at its New-Covenant height: How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?—and again, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high. The cross is the great purging: by it the Lord Jesus has accomplished the cleansing of His people once for all, putting away the sin which the blood of bulls and goats could only cover symbolically, and granting them a purged conscience to serve God in newness of life. Beyond that decisive purging, the saint is to be progressively purged in his sanctification: let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God; the vine is purged by the Husbandman (pruned) that it may bring forth more fruit; the precious metal is refined by the fire that the dross may be removed. Purging is therefore both definitive (accomplished at the cross and applied at conversion) and ongoing (the daily work of sanctification by Word and providence)—and both senses culminate in the final purging of the whole creation, when the elements shall melt with fervent heat and a new heavens and new earth shall emerge in which dwelleth righteousness.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PURGE as to cleanse or purify by separating and carrying off whatever is impure, heterogeneous, foreign, or superfluous; to clear from guilt or the imputation of guilt; in theology, to cleanse from the defilement of sin.

expand to see more

PURGE, v.t. — 1. To cleanse or purify by separating and carrying off whatever is impure, heterogeneous, foreign, or superfluous; as, to purge a liquor; to purge the body; to purge the air. 2. To clear from guilt or the imputation of guilt; as, to purge oneself from the charge of treason. 3. In theology, to cleanse from the defilement of sin; to purify from moral pollution.

PURGING, n. — The act of cleansing or purifying; the carrying off of impure or noxious matter.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 51:7 — "Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow."

Hebrews 1:3 — "Who being the brightness of his glory... when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high."

Hebrews 9:14 — "How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?"

Malachi 3:3 — "And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Purging is corrupted in the present age by its reduction to dieting fads (the ‘cleanse’ or ‘detox purge’) and to the cultural-political register of mass dismissal—both of which empty the word of its central biblical reference, the cleansing of the conscience and the soul from the defilement of sin by the blood of Christ.

expand to see more

The word purge survives in the modern vocabulary chiefly in two flattened registers. The first is dietary: the juice cleanse, the detox purge, the wellness ritual that drives the impurities out of the body and leaves the spiritually unrenewed soul untouched. The second is political-cultural: the purge of an institution’s membership, the cancellation, the ideological cleansing of those judged impure on contemporary lines. Both have their place, real or contested; neither captures the substantive biblical doctrine, in which to purge is centrally to cleanse the conscience from the defilement of sin by the blood of Christ. The wellness register treats impurity as biochemical and addresses it with kale; the political register treats impurity as ideological and addresses it with expulsion; only the gospel treats impurity as the moral pollution of a fallen heart and addresses it with the blood of the Son of God.

Recover the biblical center and the secondary uses fall into proportion. The body is to be cared for, but the cleansing the soul needs is not dietary; the church and the institution must sometimes remove the impenitent, but the cleansing the conscience needs is not procedural. The doctrine of purging is at its core the doctrine of the cross: that Christ by Himself purged our sins, that His blood cleanses from all unrighteousness, that the conscience defiled by dead works is purged by the eternal-Spirit-offered sacrifice of the Son to serve the living God. With that purging accomplished, the saint walks in the ongoing sanctifying purgation of the vine pruned by the Husbandman and the silver refined by the fire—and toward the final purgation of a creation made new.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek katharizō (to cleanse) and Hebrew kāphar (to cover, atone)—the cleansing accomplished decisively by the blood of Christ in Hebrews 1:3 and 9:14.

expand to see more

Greek katharismos (G2512) — cleansing, purification (the noun behind catharsis).

Greek katharismon poiēsas — “having made purgation”—the participle of Heb 1:3 that summarizes the cross.

Hebrew kāphar (H3722) — to cover, atone—the Day-of-Atonement verb behind the purging of the holy place.

Hebrew tāhēr (H2891) — to be clean, to cleanse—the ceremonial purity verb.
